overview: Amcor is a global leader in consumer packaging and dispensing solutions, producing flexible packaging, rigid packaging, cartons and closures for the nutrition, health, beauty and wellness end markets. Dual-listed (NYSE: AMCR primary, ASX: AMC secondary CDI) and domiciled in Jersey with a UK head office, Amcor reports in US dollars and, following its April 30, 2025 all-stock merger with Berry Global, now generates roughly $23-24 billion of annualized net sales through two segments -- Global Flexible Packaging Solutions (~72% of sales) and Global Rigid Packaging Solutions (~28%) -- operating over 400 facilities in more than 40 countries with more than 75,000 employees. The company is now mid-way through its fiscal-year-end transition from June 30 to December 31: a six-month 'Transition Period' running July 1 - December 31, 2026 (first quarter, ended September 30, 2026, already reported), with the first full calendar fiscal year ending December 31, 2027.

business_model.summary: Amcor manufactures primary packaging (the packaging that directly contains a consumer or healthcare product) under long-term customer relationships, largely on a contract/program basis with resin, aluminum and other raw-material costs passed through to customers via contractual price mechanisms. Revenue is largely repeat, non-discretionary and defensive (food, beverage, healthcare, personal care staples), though the business is not purely 'recurring' in a subscription sense -- it is high-volume, contract-manufactured B2B production tied to customers' own unit volumes. The April 2025 Berry Global merger roughly doubled net sales (from $13,640m FY2024 to $15,009m FY2025, with a full year of contribution flowing through fiscal 2026, which closed at ~$23.5bn net sales) and added ~30,000 employees, new categories (healthcare devices, dispensing, containers) and scale in North America. Through fiscal 2026 and into the Transition Period, management has also been actively pruning the combined portfolio -- six noncore businesses (~$500m of combined annual revenue) divested or agreed as of May 2026, with the ~$1.5bn North America beverage business still under active strategic review (restructuring, JV, or sale options) as of the most recent updates.

revenue_streams.name: Global Flexible Packaging Solutions
revenue_streams.description: Flexible and film packaging for food and beverage, medical/pharmaceutical, personal care and other industries; ~42,000 employees at 210 facilities in 36 countries; one of the world's largest suppliers of polymer resin, aluminum and fiber-based flexible packaging. FY2025 net sales $10,872m, EBIT margin ~13.4%.

revenue_streams.name: Global Rigid Packaging Solutions
revenue_streams.trend: growing (Berry Consumer Packaging added), with non-core units being divested
revenue_streams.description: Rigid containers, closures, dispensing and pharma delivery devices for beverage, food, healthcare and personal care; ~34,000 employees at 213 facilities in 34 countries. FY2025 net sales $4,137m (+25% reported, largely acquired), EBIT margin ~9.1%, though North American beverage sub-segment has faced operating challenges (freight/labor cost inflation) and remains under strategic review (restructuring, JV or sale) as of late 2026.

business_model.customer_type: B2B / enterprise, selling to global and regional consumer packaged goods, food & beverage, and healthcare/pharma manufacturers; no single customer exceeded 10% of consolidated net sales in the last three fiscal years, though concentration is more pronounced in certain sub-businesses
business_model.geographic_mix: North America ~51%, Western Europe ~28%, Emerging Markets ~20%, ANZ ~1% (pro forma combined basis including Berry)
business_model.end_market_mix: On the ~$20bn identified 'core' portfolio: Nutrition ~60% (protein, pet food, foodservice, liquids, other dairy), Health, Beauty & Wellness ~25% (healthcare ~13%, beauty/wellness ~12%), Specialty applications ~15% (industrial, agricultural, niche); a further ~$2.5bn of FY2025 revenue (including the North America beverage business and other smaller units) was identified for portfolio optimization/potential divestiture as less core, of which ~$500m across six businesses has already been divested or agreed by May 2026
business_model.unit_economics: Raw material costs (resin, aluminum, paper) are largely passed through contractually with a lag, so gross margin is less sensitive to commodity swings than reported revenue growth suggests; earnings growth is driven by volume, price/mix, cost productivity and, currently, Berry merger synergies rather than by expanding take rates or subscriptions. In the September-quarter 2026 (fiscal Q1 of the Transition Period), rising energy and distribution costs outpaced the pace of pricing recovery, compressing margins and driving the EPS guidance cut -- a reminder that pass-through mechanisms lag cost inflation rather than eliminate the exposure.

competitive_position.market_position: Following the Berry Global merger, Amcor describes itself as the global leader in consumer packaging and dispensing solutions for nutrition, health, beauty and wellness, with an estimated ~$23bn+ in annualized sales -- larger in scale than any single flexible or rigid packaging pure-play competitor, though the overall packaging industry remains fragmented with no single company holding a dominant global share across all formats and end markets.

moat_factors.description: Over 400 facilities in 40+ countries lets Amcor serve multinational CPG and healthcare customers locally/regionally with consistent quality and service, a significant barrier for smaller regional converters bidding for global accounts

Especially in healthcare and pharma packaging, customer qualification, regulatory approval and validated supply chains create high switching costs and long, sticky contract relationships once a packaging format is designed into a customer's product

~$180m annual R&D spend, over 1,500 R&D professionals, 10 innovation centers and 5,000+ patents/patent applications support differentiated, sustainability-oriented packaging formats (mono-material recyclable structures, paper-based alternatives) that are difficult for smaller players to replicate at scale

Amcor was the first major packaging company (2018) to commit to fully recyclable/compostable/reusable packaging by 2025 and continues to invest in recycle-ready formats; this can be a moat where large CPG customers require sustainability credentials from suppliers, though the company acknowledges not all competitors face equivalent ESG cost burdens

The combined entity spans flexible film, rigid containers, closures and dispensing/delivery devices across more materials (polymer, paper, aluminum) than most single-format competitors, allowing broader cross-selling and one-stop-shop positioning with large multinational customers; management cites roughly $140 million of newly won business as of September 2026 as early evidence of this cross-sell benefit

weaknesses: Commodity, contract-manufacturing economics: limited pricing power versus raw material suppliers or large customers; EBIT margins in the low-to-mid teens (Flexibles) or high single digits (Rigids) are structurally thin versus higher-moat industrials, and the fiscal Q1 2026-27 (Sept-quarter) results showed pricing lagging energy/distribution cost inflation
No meaningful network effects or platform dynamics -- growth is largely volume- and price/mix-driven, tied to underlying customer unit sales

North American beverage rigid packaging sub-segment has underperformed (operating disruptions, freight/labor cost inflation) and remains unresolved -- still under strategic review more than a year after being flagged as non-core

Substantial integration complexity and execution risk from digesting a target (Berry) that materially changed Amcor's size, culture and geographic mix, now compounded by a fiscal-year-end change and a new board chair

High financial leverage post-merger (leverage ended the September 2026 quarter at ~3.76x net debt/adjusted EBITDA) constrains near-term capital allocation flexibility relative to less-levered packaging peers

growth_drivers: Berry Global merger synergies: total identified synergies of $650 million (pre-tax) targeted by the end of fiscal/calendar 2028, comprising ~$530m cost synergies, ~$60m financial savings and ~$60m growth synergies; $285 million captured in FY2026 (~10% ahead of the initial ~$260m year-one target), directly accretive to adjusted EPS

New business wins: management cited approximately $140 million of newly captured business as of September 2026, expected to phase into revenue over coming quarters, partly enabled by the broader combined product portfolio

Portfolio optimization: six noncore businesses (~$500m of combined annual revenue) divested or agreed by May 2026; the North America beverage business (~$1.5bn of revenue) remains under active review for restructuring, JV or sale, which would further reallocate capital toward higher-growth, higher-margin categories (healthcare, beauty & wellness, pet food, foodservice, liquids, protein)

Secular demand growth in target end markets: healthcare packaging is growing faster than most other verticals; pet food, protein and liquids categories provide resilient, largely non-discretionary volume growth; organic volumes grew for a fourth consecutive quarter in the September 2026 quarter (+1%, focus categories +3%)

Continued innovation in recyclable/mono-material and paper-based packaging formats (AmPrima, AmFiber, AmSky, Perflex) to meet customer sustainability commitments and potentially command premium positioning as ESG/EPR regulation tightens

Deleveraging path: management guided to leverage declining to approximately 3x net debt/EBITDA by the end of calendar 2027 (from ~3.76x at September 2026 quarter-end, expected ~3.6x by Transition Period end), which should progressively free up cash for increased shareholder returns and/or bolt-on M&A

Working capital recovery: management expects to recover more than $500 million of working capital tied up due to Middle East conflict-related disruptions, with roughly $800 million of positive free cash flow expected in the December 2026 quarter alone as the cost/pricing timing gap and inventory build unwind

business.description: Combining two large, complex organizations (harmonizing systems, retaining talent, integrating IT/controls, realizing synergies) could take longer or cost more than planned; Amcor explicitly excluded Berry from its FY2025 internal-controls assessment given the transaction closed in Q4
No single customer exceeds 10% of sales, but consolidation among large CPG/retail customers increases pricing pressure and bargaining power in certain sub-businesses
Highly competitive, fragmented industry with competition on price, innovation, sustainability, service and quality; disruptive technologies from competitors could erode Amcor's position

Operating disruptions and cost inflation at high-volume sites in the non-core beverage business remain unresolved more than a year after being flagged; management continues to cite only 'encouraging discussions' without a closed transaction, prolonging the drag on consolidated Rigids margins

In the September 2026 quarter, rising energy and distribution costs outpaced pricing recovery, directly causing the Transition Period EPS guidance cut; management says it expects to close this gap by the December 2026 quarter-end, but repeated misses on this dynamic would signal a structural, not just timing, issue
Shifts away from certain plastic formats due to environmental or regulatory pressure could reduce demand for some legacy products faster than Amcor can pivot its portfolio

financial.description: Net debt/adjusted EBITDA leverage was ~3.76x at the end of the September 2026 quarter, guided toward ~3.6x by the Transition Period year-end (December 31, 2026) and toward ~3x by the end of calendar 2027; increased indebtedness could pressure credit ratings, raise borrowing costs, and constrain flexibility to fund operations or shareholder returns

$18.7 billion of goodwill and other intangible assets after the merger as of June 30, 2025; adverse changes in cost of capital, market multiples or expected cash flows could trigger material non-cash impairment charges
A meaningful minority of indebtedness is at variable rates; rising rates increase debt service costs on that portion and could raise the cost of refinancing fixed-rate debt

FY2026 free cash flow guidance was cut twice (from $1.8-1.9bn to ~$1.3bn actual), and the newly issued Transition Period adjusted EPS guidance was then cut again just one quarter in (from $1.80-1.90 to $1.70-1.80) alongside a Q1 EPS miss ($0.95 actual vs. $1.04 consensus) -- a pattern across two consecutive guidance periods that raises forecasting-credibility questions during the integration

Reports in USD but has material exposure to EUR, BRL, CHF, CNY and GBP; translational and transactional FX moves affect reported results, and currency devaluation (e.g., Argentina, treated as highly inflationary under US GAAP) can create lagged cost pass-through issues

regulatory.description: Extended producer responsibility (EPR) programs, potential plastic bans/restrictions, new packaging taxes and PFAS restrictions (multiple US states) could raise compliance costs, require costly reformulation, or close off certain markets; not all competitors face equivalent ESG-driven cost burdens, potentially disadvantaging Amcor on cost even as it maintains sustainability leadership

2025 US reciprocal tariff actions raised the effective US tariff rate to multi-decade highs; while Amcor has generally been able to pass through tariff costs historically, further escalation or retroactive customs disputes could pressure margins or demand
15% global minimum tax framework phasing in across jurisdictions where Amcor operates; not currently expected to be material but subject to ongoing guidance changes
Significant portion of revenue from highly regulated healthcare and food/beverage packaging; non-compliance risk includes fines, license revocation, and litigation

macro.description: Cited directly by management as a driver of elevated inventory levels, working capital drag, and repeated free cash flow guidance cuts through FY2026; recovery of $500m+ of related working capital is a stated but still only partly realized tailwind, with ~$800m of free cash flow expected to land in the December 2026 quarter

Polymer resins, aluminum, paper and energy costs are subject to substantial fluctuation from geopolitical risk, inflation and supply chain disruption; while largely pass-through, timing lags compressed margins in the September 2026 quarter specifically via rising energy and distribution costs

Demand depends on customers' end-consumer sales volumes; a broad economic slowdown, even in defensive categories like food and healthcare, could soften volumes, though volumes have now improved for four consecutive quarters through September 2026
~20% of pro forma sales from Emerging Markets exposes Amcor to currency devaluation risk (e.g., Argentina hyperinflationary accounting) and political/economic instability

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The global packaging industry is estimated at roughly $1.3 trillion in 2026, growing toward ~$1.75 trillion by 2035. Flexible packaging (~$330bn market) is growing at a mid-single-digit CAGR (~4-6%), with healthcare packaging and mono-material/recyclable formats among the fastest-growing sub-segments; rigid packaging (~40% of the format mix) is sustained by recyclable bottle, container and tray demand across food, beverage and personal care. The industry is navigating a complex mix of tightening sustainability regulation, consumer affordability pressure, and an evolving tariff landscape into 2027.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate -- packaging demand is tied to defensive end markets (food, beverage, healthcare, personal care) that are less cyclical than durable goods, though volumes still soften in broader economic slowdowns and the North American beverage/rigid sub-segment has shown more cyclicality recently
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high in the near term given elevated post-merger leverage (~3.76x at September 2026 quarter-end); a portion of debt is variable-rate, and deleveraging toward ~3x by end of calendar 2027 is a key management priority to reduce this sensitivity over time
macro_factors.currency_exposure: High -- USD reporting currency against material EUR, BRL, CHF, CNY and GBP exposures, plus Argentina hyperinflationary accounting; ~20% of pro forma sales come from Emerging Markets
macro_factors.regulatory_environment: Increasingly stringent globally on plastics, extended producer responsibility, PFAS restrictions and climate/ESG disclosure; Amcor's early sustainability commitments (2018 pledge on recyclable/compostable/reusable packaging by 2025, science-based net-zero-by-2050 targets being re-baselined post-Berry) position it to compete for ESG-conscious customers but do not eliminate rising compliance costs across a fragmented, non-harmonized global regulatory landscape.

recent_developments.event: Completed all-stock merger with Berry Global Group (7.25 Amcor shares per Berry share), closing ahead of the original schedule; Berry delisted from NYSE. Established Amcor as the global leader in consumer packaging and dispensing solutions for nutrition, health, beauty and wellness.

Reported FY2025 GAAP net sales of $15,009m (+10%) and adjusted EPS of 71.2 cents (+3%); flagged ~$2.5bn of revenue (including the ~$1.5bn North America beverage business) as non-core and under strategic review.

Reported Q3 FY2026 net sales of $5.91bn (+77.4%); cut FY2026 free cash flow guidance from $1.8-1.9bn to $1.5-1.6bn citing elevated inventory tied to Middle East conflict-related disruption; disclosed six noncore business divestitures/agreements totaling ~$500m of annual revenue and 'encouraging discussions' on the North America beverage business; announced the fiscal-year-end change to December 31 and a new Miami HQ for select corporate functions plus a PwC US auditor change.

Reported FY2026 net sales of ~$23.5bn (+57% YoY) and adjusted EPS of $4.02 (+13% YoY); free cash flow of $1.303bn, below the original $1.8-1.9bn guidance. Raised the quarterly dividend to $0.65/share (from $0.6375). Synergies of $285m captured in FY2026, ~10% ahead of target. Issued initial Transition Period (H2 CY2026) guidance of $1.80-1.90 adjusted diluted EPS and year-end leverage of 3.5x-3.6x; flagged double-digit adjusted EPS growth expected for calendar 2027.
JPMorgan downgraded Amcor from Overweight to Neutral (price target raised to $47 from $44), citing concerns over slowing EBITDA growth amid the divestiture program and rising capex.

Announced a board chair transition: Graeme Liebelt, chair for nearly 13 years, will not stand for re-election and will be succeeded by Tom Long, an independent director since 2017 and former MillerCoors CEO, effective at the November 11, 2026 annual meeting. Coverage tied the change to the scale of post-Berry integration.

recent_developments.date: 2026-11-04/05 (Q1 Transition Period results, quarter ended September 30, 2026)
recent_developments.event: Reported net sales of $6.129bn (+7% YoY) ahead of the ~$5.90bn consensus, but adjusted EPS of $0.95 missed the $1.04 consensus. Organic volumes grew ~1% (fourth consecutive quarter of sequential improvement; focus categories +3%), but rising energy and distribution costs outpaced pricing recovery, compressing margins. Cut the newly issued Transition Period adjusted EPS guidance to $1.70-1.80 from $1.80-1.90. Leverage ended the quarter at ~3.76x net debt/adjusted EBITDA, guided to ~3.6x by Transition Period end and ~3x by end of calendar 2027. Free cash flow is expected to be roughly neutral for the Transition Period as a whole, with ~$800m of positive free cash flow expected in the December 2026 quarter alone as the cost/pricing timing gap closes. Board raised the quarterly dividend further to $0.66/share. Management reiterated double-digit adjusted EPS growth expected for calendar 2027.
Annual general meeting held in London; Tom Long formally took over as Board Chair from Graeme Liebelt.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO Peter Konieczny, CFO Stephen Scherger) framed the September-quarter (fiscal Q1 of the Transition Period) results as a revenue beat but an EPS miss driven specifically by energy and distribution cost inflation outpacing pricing recovery -- a timing issue they expect to close by the December 2026 quarter-end, not a change to the underlying demand or synergy trajectory. They reiterated double-digit adjusted EPS growth for calendar 2027, continued progress on Berry integration and the ~$650m synergy target, and a further dividend increase to $0.66/share, even as the Transition Period EPS guidance was cut and leverage came in modestly above plan at ~3.76x. The ~$1.5bn North America beverage business remains under active strategic review (restructuring, JV, or sale) with no transaction announced as of the most recent update, and six smaller noncore businesses (~$500m combined revenue) have already been divested or agreed. A new Board Chair, Tom Long, took over from long-serving Chair Graeme Liebelt at the November 11, 2026 AGM.

bull_case: Berry Global merger synergies are tracking ahead of schedule ($285m captured in FY2026 vs. an original ~$260m target, out of a $650m multi-year target), directly accretive to adjusted EPS and provides a multi-year, largely self-funded earnings growth runway independent of end-market volume growth

Organic volumes have now grown for four consecutive quarters through September 2026 (focus categories +3%), suggesting the defensive, non-discretionary end markets (food, beverage, healthcare, personal care) are stabilizing demand even as the company prunes its portfolio

Management has continued raising the dividend twice within 2026 (to $0.65 then $0.66/share) despite EPS and free cash flow guidance cuts, signaling confidence in the underlying cash generation and supporting a current dividend yield in the mid-single digits

Portfolio optimization is actively progressing -- six noncore businesses (~$500m revenue) already divested or agreed, with the ~$1.5bn North America beverage business still in play -- which could reallocate capital toward higher-growth, higher-margin categories and improve consolidated margins over time

Deleveraging path remains intact (leverage guided toward ~3.6x by Transition Period end and ~3x by end of calendar 2027 despite the Q1 overshoot to ~3.76x), which should progressively unlock capital for buybacks, M&A or further dividend growth as the balance sheet normalizes post-merger
bear_case: Guidance credibility is now a two-period pattern, not a one-off: FY2026 free cash flow guidance was cut twice (to ~$1.3bn actual from an original $1.8-1.9bn), and the brand-new Transition Period adjusted EPS guidance was already cut from $1.80-1.90 to $1.70-1.80 just one quarter in, alongside an EPS miss versus consensus ($0.95 vs. $1.04) -- raising real forecasting risk during a critical integration window

Elevated post-merger leverage (~3.76x net debt/adjusted EBITDA at the September 2026 quarter-end, above the prior ~3.5-3.6x full-year guide) limits near-term financial flexibility and remains sensitive to interest rates and to the pace/success of synergy realization and cash generation

The North America beverage business has now been under strategic review for well over a year with no closed transaction -- 'encouraging discussions' but no deal -- continuing to weigh on consolidated Rigids segment margins and tying up management attention

Structurally thin, largely pass-through contract-manufacturing economics (EBIT margins in the high single digits to mid-teens) leave limited room for error, and the September 2026 quarter demonstrated this directly: rising energy and distribution costs outpaced pricing recovery and drove the guidance cut

Integration risk remains material and is compounded by concurrent organizational change: combining Amcor and Berry's systems, cultures, and controls; a simultaneous fiscal-year-end change to calendar year; a corporate relocation of select functions to a new Miami headquarters; a new external auditor (PwC US); and, as of November 2026, a new Board Chair succeeding a 13-year incumbent -- a high degree of concurrent change that increases near-term execution risk

Intensifying plastics/ESG and EPR regulation (PFAS restrictions, potential plastic bans/taxes) could raise compliance costs unevenly across competitors, and secular pressure on certain flexible plastic formats could erode demand for parts of the legacy Amcor and Berry product lines faster than reformulation efforts can offset
